questions.q: What does 'storytelling with data' mean, according to this lesson?
options: Choosing visuals that support one clear point, rather than using different chart types just to show variety
Adding as many visual types as possible to a single report page
Only using pie charts because they look approachable
Writing a narrative text box on every page
questions.explain: A report page should communicate a clear point at a glance — variety for its own sake adds friction rather than clarity.

questions.q: Why should you avoid mixing large and small measures on the same chart axis?
options: Power BI cannot technically render two different scales
Mixing scales is always fine as long as both use the same color
The smaller series can look flat even when it's moving significantly, distorting the comparison
It's only a problem with pie charts, not line charts
questions.explain: A series in the thousands next to one in the millions gets visually flattened — a second axis (combo chart) fixes this instead of forcing both onto one scale.

questions.q: How does sorting a chart by measure differ from sorting it by category?
options: They produce identical results in every case
Sorting by measure highlights the highest or lowest values; sorting by category helps viewers quickly locate one specific item among many
Sorting by measure removes the need for axis labels
Sorting by category is only available on tables, not charts
questions.explain: The choice of sort order changes what a viewer notices first — it's a storytelling decision, not just a cosmetic default.

questions.q: What's the recommended way to display large numbers for readability?
options: Display numbers as percentages only
Always show every digit for maximum precision
Keep displayed numbers to three or four significant digits, scaling for thousands or millions (e.g. '3.4 million' instead of '3,400,000')
Round every number to the nearest whole number regardless of scale
questions.explain: Fewer significant digits read faster and more accurately — showing every digit of a large number adds noise without adding useful precision.

questions.q: Why are 3D charts and charts with a truncated (non-zero) axis considered distortions?
options: Both make differences between values look bigger or smaller than they actually are
They only cause problems when printed in black and white
They are simply outdated visual styles with no functional issue
3D charts are always more accurate than 2D charts
questions.explain: These techniques visually exaggerate or minimize real differences in the data, misleading a viewer about the actual scale of a comparison.
